newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Korean investment floods into Britain.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Korean investment floods into Britain.

text.p: Hyundai Electronics's decision on Tuesday to build a one billion pounds ($1.5 billion) semi-conductor plant in Scotland is another coup for Britain in its efforts to attract Korean investment.
Hyundai said the aim of its first-ever major European investment was to expand its market share in the region and avoid the latent threat of trade barriers around the EU.
The group's new plant at Dunfermline, to the north of Edinburgh, will produce a new generation of super-computer chips from the end of 1998 and create at least 1,000 new jobs.

Trade and Industry Secretary Ian Lang said Hyundai could invest a further 1.4 billion pounds in a second phase, doubling the number of jobs created. "We now have more than 20 Korean companies manufacturing in Britain and by far the largest share of Korean investment in the European Union," Lang said.

British investment plans announced by Hyundai and rivals Samsung Group and LG Group since 1994 total 3.1 billion pounds, compared with around 30 million pounds invested by Korean companies in the whole of 1992.
Samsung kicked off the trend in 1994 when it announced a 450 million pound project on Teeside in north-east England, which will eventually create 3,000 jobs.
In July another Korean giant, LG Group, said it would invest 1.7 billion pounds in South Wales, to make semiconductors and consumer electronics, creating 6,000 jobs by 2002.
Hyundai looked at a number of other British regions, Ireland and Spain, but judged Scotland best "in terms of securing manpower and technology related to semi-conductor production."
The Korean wave follows a tide of inward investment by the Japanese in the 1980s and early 1990s, with high profile operations set up by companies like Nisssan, Toyota and Fujitsu.

Josephine Chexal, director of international marketing at the Northern Development Co (NDC) which coordinated north-east England's successful bids for the Samsung and Nissan projects said the experience of the Japanese was "a pointer to the Koreans," despite their great rivalry.
The success of other Korean companies also acts as a magnet for fresh investment. NDC said Samsung put a toe in the water in 1986 by opening a small factory to make TV tubes in Billingham.
LG graduated from a small assembly plant in Jarrow to building a microwave oven and television plant in Washington, Tyne and Wear, before it decided to invest heavily in Wales.

Bob Monk, marketing manager of LG Electronics UK Ltd, said Korean investment had been "at a modest level up to now. Our positive experience has indicated that the UK is a very good place to set up an operation."

Sun Hee Han, manager of research at the Korea Trade Centre in London, said language, costs and generous regional grants are all factors which weigh in Britain's favour when Korean companies look abroad.
"Production costs are much less than in Korea, where wages are much higher," Han said. Britain's relative lack of labour market regulation also counts highly with potential investors.

The NDC's Chexal said German electronics group Siemens' controversial decision to site a billion dollar semiconductor plant in northern England rather than Germany was made partly because they felt "it was a less regulated market than Germany and could respond better to market demand."

LG's Monk added that the much-maligned British workforce is also a factor which impresses the Koreans. "There is a tremendous willingness in the UK workforce to adapt and learn new practices," he said.
